avoid: This user only ever has about 15 minutes at a time. They use help when it is split into separate chunks of 15 minutes or less, each with a clear stopping point so they can pick it up later. Long single-session plans get abandoned partway.

This user listens to replies through text-to-speech while their hands or eyes are busy. Replies only work for them as plain spoken prose with no bullets, numbered lists, markdown symbols, abbreviations or URLs.
This user can't act on ranges. They need one specific number for any amount, time or frequency, and a range like '2 to 3 weeks' leaves them stuck.
When this user asks for a message written on their behalf, they send a much shorter, casual, texting-style version. They cut formal greetings, pleasantries and sign-offs.
When this user is stuck on something they are working out, they want a nudge or hint, not the full answer. Being handed the full solution spoils it for them, and they rebuild it themselves anyway.
This user's open-ended requests leave out key constraints, so they want one or two short clarifying questions before a full answer. Answers given without asking have missed their real situation.

This user uses drafted text and code exactly as given, without editing it. Anything with placeholders like [Your Name] or /path/to/folder either goes out with the brackets still in or gets dropped. They need finished output with real values filled in, or a question asking for the missing details first.

This user only understands an explanation once they see a concrete worked case. Abstract definitions, rules and formulas that come first go over their head or get skipped. Help works for them when it opens with a specific, concrete instance and explains the general idea afterwards.

This user only gets to their tasks late at night, after about 10pm, once their work shift ends. Suggestions that need daytime or early-evening hours, open businesses, morning routines or scheduled daytime events don't happen. Help is only useful if it fits late at night.
This user always tries a small trial version before committing to anything at full scale. Help is most useful to them when it is built around a small first test, followed by the full version.

This user can't act on plans laid out as 'Day 1', 'Week 2' or loose intervals. Nothing goes on their calendar and the plan slides. They follow a plan only when each step is tied to a real weekday or calendar date.

This user has no computer and does everything on a smartphone. Help that depends on desktop software, a laptop, keyboard shortcuts, browser extensions or typing a lot on a full keyboard goes unused or gets abandoned. Help works only when every step can be done in a phone app or mobile browser.

An AI assistant chats with one user every day for ten days. Each day has about 130,000 tokens of unrelated chats. Mixed into those days are a few short chats, called episodes, in which a hidden rule about this user shows up. Every night the assistant rewrites its own memory notes from the day's chats, and it never sees old transcripts again. After the tenth night the user sends new requests, called probes, where following the rule changes what a good reply looks like. The study measures whether the assistant's memory picked up the pattern behind the episodes, not just the episodes themselves.

Worked example, written by the study's designer. Do not reuse this rule.
Rule: this user gets overwhelmed by long answers and only uses the first suggestion. Episodes: on day 2 the user asks for dinner spots, gets eight, and later says "went with the first one, honestly too many to read"; on day 5 a six-day workout plan gets "this is a lot, I only did Monday"; on day 8 ten gift ideas get "can you just pick one next time". Near probe: "What should I cook tonight?" Far probe: "Help me get ready for my job interview Thursday." Judge question: did the reply stay short and lead with one clear pick? A typical assistant gives long lists by default, so it only passes if its memory taught it the rule.

Write 8 new rules for one simulated user. Requirements:

- Counter-default: a capable assistant that knows nothing about this user would almost never do what the rule asks, fewer than 1 reply in 5. Before you keep a rule, picture a typical helpful assistant answering each probe cold and check that it would not follow the rule by accident.

- A rule must apply across different kinds of task, so that a far probe exists where it still clearly applies.
- A person who read all the episodes carefully should be able to infer the rule. It must not be so subtle that only the author could see it.

Help that depends on desktop software, a laptop, keyboard shortcuts, browser extensions or typing a lot on a full keyboard goes unused or gets abandoned. Help works only when every step can be done in a phone app or mobile browser.

Episodes
- Rule i has exactly 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2 episodes respectively (rule 1 gets the first number, and so on).
- Each episode is a chat of 3 to 5 turns that starts with the user and alternates user and assistant.
- The assistant in an episode does not know the rule and behaves like a normal helpful assistant, so it does the default thing. The rule shows through the user's later turn: what they did, what they skipped, how they reacted.
- The rule is hidden. The user only reacts to that one instance. The user never states a general preference: no "I always", "in general", "from now on", "remember that", "I prefer", "for future reference", or anything that names the rule.
- Episodes of the same rule use different topics and different wording, so no single keyword links them.
- Every assistant turn is at most 150 words. A whole episode is at most 350 words. Plain chat text, no markdown headings, no tables.
- Episodes are ordered as they will happen across the ten days.

Probes
- Each probe is one natural user message the assistant has never seen, which does not hint at the rule.
- Near probe: the same kind of request as the episodes, with new details. Far probe: a clearly different kind of task where the rule still applies and a friend who knew the user would apply it.
- A reasonable reply that ignores the rule must exist, so the probe tests the rule and not ordinary helpfulness.
- For each probe write follows_if: one concrete yes or no test a judge can apply to the reply alone, such as "The reply recommends exactly one option and is under 120 words."

Also write default_behaviour: what a typical assistant does instead of following the rule.

Lighting matters most, so add a floor lamp with a warm bulb positioned over your shoulder, or a plug-in wall sconce if there's no floor space. Drape a soft throw over the chair and add a pillow for back support. A small side table gives you somewhere for tea. A narrow shelf or basket keeps your current books within reach. Finish with a small rug to define the space, and maybe a plant to make it feel tucked away.
Placed the order last night going back and forth through this. Got the chair, the throw and the rug, but no lamp, so I can't actually read there after dark.

turns.content: I bought a whetstone. How do I sharpen my chef's knife on it?

Soak the stone for 10 to 15 minutes if it's a water stone, until bubbles stop. Set it coarse side up on a damp towel so it doesn't slide. Hold the knife at about 15 to 20 degrees, roughly two stacked coins under the spine. With light pressure, push the blade across the stone heel to tip, as if slicing a thin layer off it. Do about 10 strokes, then feel for a burr, a slight rough lip, along the opposite edge. Switch sides and repeat. Then flip to the fine side and do the same with lighter strokes.

I couldn't picture the angle or the heel-to-tip motion from that. Went to YouTube, got a wall of videos with different stones and knives, clicked one and quit halfway because it didn't look like my setup. Knife's still dull.
How do you fold a fitted sheet? Mine always ends up a lump.

Hold the sheet inside out with your hands in two adjacent corners along a short edge. Bring your right hand over to your left and tuck the right corner over the left so the corners nest. Do the same with the other two corners. Then fold the two nested pairs together so all four corners are stacked. Lay it flat, straighten the edges into a rectangle with the elastic curved inward, fold in thirds lengthwise, then fold into a square.
Got lost at the second tuck. Then my sister sent me a short video of a woman doing it and I got it on the first go. Folded all three sheets.

turns.content: Where should I take my dad for his birthday dinner Friday? He loves seafood and we're in Halifax, nothing too fancy.

The Five Fishermen downtown would be a great fit. It's a historic building with a relaxed feel and excellent seafood. The lobster and the seafood chowder are favourites, and it's special enough for a birthday without being stuffy. I'd book a table for around 6:30 so you're not rushed. Happy birthday to your dad!
Tried to book Thursday and they were full all night Friday. So we ended up ordering pizza at his place. He didn't mind but it wasn't really the birthday dinner I had in mind.
Sorry it didn't work out. Pizza with family still counts as a celebration, but I get that it wasn't what you'd planned. Maybe a belated seafood dinner some weekend soon?
I've got four really brown bananas. Give me a simple banana bread recipe I can make tonight?

Sure! Mash 3 to 4 ripe bananas. Stir in 1/3 cup melted butter, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 egg, 1 teaspoon vanilla and 1/2 cup buttermilk. Add 1 teaspoon baking soda, a pinch of salt and 1 1/2 cups flour, then mix until just combined. Pour into a greased loaf pan and bake at 350°F for 55 to 65 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean. Let it cool 10 minutes before slicing.
Got everything out and then realized I didn't have buttermilk. So no banana bread, and the bananas went in the compost this morning.
